passA.summary: Sanja Grbic, a product designer at Automattic, recounts "Radical Speed Month" — a company experiment where roadmap work was paused for 30 days and two-person teams were given full autonomy to build and ship something real. About a third of the company (~500 people) participated in the first round, starting roughly 794 projects. She walks through three projects she personally built, tracing her shift from a designer who had never shipped code at work to someone deploying an internal tool to production in a large, security-gated system. The talk's real argument is organizational rather than technical: AI velocity in a 1,400-person company with decades-old software depends less on the tools than on enablement, agency, and space to experiment. Watch it if you care about how non-engineers actually cross into code inside a big org, and what engineers' roles become when they do.
key_points: Automattic paused roadmap work for 30 days and had ~500 people (a third of the company, in staged rounds) pair up and ship real projects with full autonomy; AI use was encouraged but not required.

The enabling infrastructure predated the experiment: a two-week role-specific AI course for every employee, security and dev-environment setup good enough for non-engineers, and an MCP server ("context AC") exposing decades of internal documentation to AI tools.

In a two-hour group exercise, a mixed team of two designers, an engineer, and a product lead shipped a working board-game session manager using Claude Code plus Nano Banana for illustration — with the engineer's main contribution being to set up Git and unblock the others.
Grbic's central claim for engineers: enabling teammates who are newly working in code can produce more impact than doing more engineering yourself.

Her main project, a design system status tracker, was proposed over an engineer's concerns about performance, maintenance, and feasibility; she built it solo as a proof of concept in about 2.5 weeks and shipped it internally and on a public-facing site.

The process inversion is the concrete takeaway: prototype in code first, then return to Figma late for mood boards and visual fine-tuning, rather than working in Figma to high fidelity before building.

The third project — an iOS chat app for WooCommerce merchants with wordpress.com auth, a site-themed widget, and an AI agent that answers visitor questions and knows when it can't — went zero to working proof of concept in six days, because both designers had already leveled up.

Her prescription for large organizations: give people tool access, find enablers and champions, create space for experimentation, and grant agency — because changing process in a big company means changing human behavior, not just tooling.

notable_quotes.text: The instructions were to pause the roadmap work for 30 days, pair with a partner, and ship something real. We were welcome to use AI, though it wasn't a requirement.
notable_quotes.why: The experiment's design in one line, including the notable fact that AI was optional.

notable_quotes.text: We had about a third of the company participating in the first round. That's around 500 people that started around 794 projects in these 30 days.
notable_quotes.why: The headline numbers behind the talk's title.

notable_quotes.text: if you're an engineer, the impact that you have when you enable others may be far greater than the impact of doing more engineering yourself
notable_quotes.why: The talk's sharpest position, and one plenty of engineers would push back on.

notable_quotes.text: this was the biggest learning for me, uh that engineers will need to become enablers and teachers
notable_quotes.why: States the role change as a prediction, not just an observation.

notable_quotes.text: now with AI, we can all do a little bit um of the work that's outside of our domain
notable_quotes.why: Compact statement of the premise the whole talk rests on.

notable_quotes.text: no matter what role uses AI, um this velocity is going to look very different in small teams like one to three people that are building new products
notable_quotes.why: Frames the small-team vs. large-org distinction that separates this talk from typical vibe-coding demos.

notable_quotes.text: It's an MCP server that gives AI tools access to all of the knowledge and data that we have documented over the years
notable_quotes.why: Names the specific institutional-knowledge plumbing that made non-engineer contribution viable.

notable_quotes.text: I had never until then actually built and shipped something in code. And I mean at work.
notable_quotes.why: Establishes the baseline that makes the rest of the story measurable.

notable_quotes.text: the solution that I proposed raised questions with the engineer around performance, around maintenance, and if we would be able to to build it in the first place
notable_quotes.why: Names the friction point AI let her route around — a real tradeoff, not a success story.

notable_quotes.text: the discovery portion was three people, but the design and build was just myself. And it took around 2 and 1/2 weeks to build this.
notable_quotes.why: Concrete team size and duration for the flagship project.

notable_quotes.text: delivering this this product was a defining moment for me, where I moved from a designer to a design engineer. This is of course enabled by AI, but most of all, it was enabled by the fact that I could own the entire process.
notable_quotes.why: Explicitly ranks organizational agency above the tooling as the causal factor.

notable_quotes.text: I could just build whatever I thought was um was needed, and I didn't have to spend a lot of time in negotiations and handover
notable_quotes.why: Identifies coordination overhead, not implementation speed, as the thing that was removed.

notable_quotes.text: In only 6 days, we went from zero to uh through the entire process to building an iOS chat for WooCommerce merchants
notable_quotes.why: The compounding-speed data point that closes the arc.

notable_quotes.text: we started the exploration as a cloud code project folder where all of the chats and ideas were recorded into a file system. And I I noticed that that um significantly uh sped up collaboration
notable_quotes.why: A specific, portable workflow practice she kept after the experiment.

notable_quotes.text: that's the biggest shift for our process because normally we would start in Figma and we would work in Figma until we reach very high fidelity
in only 30 days, my process that has been similar for years has completely shifted. And that was true for many other people.
notable_quotes.why: Claims the individual change generalized across participants.

notable_quotes.text: here I'm talking about being able to push code to production in a well-established large system that requires serious onboarding and security practices
notable_quotes.why: Preempts the obvious objection that this was only toy projects.

notable_quotes.text: changing processes or tools in large organizations requires shifting the human behavior behind them
notable_quotes.why: The thesis of the talk, stated as the closing prescription.

positions.claim: An engineer's impact from enabling non-engineer teammates can exceed the impact of doing more engineering themselves.
Engineers' roles will need to shift from builders to enablers and teachers as more non-engineers work in code.
The primary enabler of her shift to design engineer was owning the entire process and having agency, more than the AI tooling itself.
AI-driven velocity looks fundamentally different in 1-3 person zero-to-one teams than in organizations of thousands with 5-20 year old software.
Designers should build the working prototype first and return to Figma only later for visual fine-tuning, inverting the traditional high-fidelity-mockup-first workflow.
Recording exploration chats and ideas into a Claude Code project folder file system significantly speeds up both collaboration and subsequent building.
Adopting AI tools in a large organization is a human behavior change problem, so tool access alone is insufficient without champions, experimentation space, and agency.
Removing risk from a project (building something unrelated to existing products) is what allowed the team to focus on learning.
Well-documented asynchronous work practices are a prerequisite for making internal knowledge usefully accessible to AI tools.
A non-engineer can ship to production in a large legacy system when systems and operations teams have invested in security, process, and documentation quality.
